p117: 117.  Thus, in the Court’s view, the refusal to take into account such an allegation, substantiated by the applicant by means of a certificate issued by a professional whose conclusions disclosed the possible existence of a grave risk within the meaning of Article 13 (b) of the Hague Convention, was contrary to the requirements of Article 8 of the Convention. The fact that the expert report had not been prepared in adversarial proceedings was not sufficient to exempt the courts from examining it effectively, since the Regional Court, in the exercise of its judicial function, could have submitted the document for discussion between the parties, or even ordered of its own motion a court-appointed expert report in adversarial proceedings – which Latvian law permits (see paragraph 45 above). The question whether the mother could follow her daughter to Australia and maintain contact with her should also have been addressed. The Court emphasises, moreover, that in any event, as the rights guaranteed by Article 8 of the Convention, which forms part of Latvian law and is directly applicable, constitute “fundamental principles of the requested State relating to the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms” within the meaning of Article 20 of the Hague Convention, the Regional Court could not dispense with such a review in the circumstances of the case.
p118: 118.  As to the need to comply with the short time-limits laid down by the Hague Convention and referred to by the Rīga Regional Court in its reasoning (see paragraph 25 above), the Court reiterates that while Article 11 of the Hague Convention does indeed provide that the judicial authorities must act expeditiously, this does not exonerate them from the duty to undertake an effective examination of allegations made by a party on the basis of one of the exceptions expressly provided for, namely Article 13 (b) in this case.
p119: 119.  In view of the foregoing, the Court considers that the applicant suffered a disproportionate interference with her right to respect for her family life, in that the decision-making process under domestic law did not satisfy the procedural requirements inherent in Article 8 of the Convention, the Rīga Regional Court having failed to carry out an effective examination of the applicant’s allegations under Article 13 (b) of the Hague Convention.
p120: 120.  There has accordingly been a violation of Article 8 of the Convention.
p122: 122.  As the applicant did not submit any claim in respect of non-pecuniary or pecuniary damage, the Court considers that there is no call to award her any sum on that account.
p123: 123.  The applicant claimed 1,996.91 lati, that is, 2,858.84 euros (EUR), for the costs and expenses incurred before the Grand Chamber of the Court, producing a number of supporting documents.
p124: 124.  The Government considered that the applicant’s claims were neither justified nor reasonable, with the exception of a sum of EUR 485.19 in respect of the expenses incurred for the travel of the applicant’s representative in order to attend the hearing before the Court.
p125: 125.  The Court reiterates that an applicant is entitled to the reimbursement of costs and expenses only in so far as it has been shown that these have been actually and necessarily incurred and are reasonable as to quantum. In the present case, regard being had to the documents in its possession and to its case-law, the Court considers it reasonable to award the applicant the sum of EUR 2,000 for costs and expenses in the proceedings before it.
p126: 126.  The Court considers it appropriate that the default interest rate should be based on the marginal lending rate of the European Central Bank, to which should be added three percentage points.
